unit.title: Speaking and listening: adapting language and turn-taking

objectives.text: Use appropriate phrases and registers, and adapt contributions to take account of purpose, audience and medium.
Respect the turn-taking rights of others during discussions, using the appropriate language for interjections.

lesson.title: Adapting Language and Turn-Taking in Discussions
lesson.summary: This lesson explores how to adjust your language for different audiences and media while maintaining respectful turn-taking. Learners will identify appropriate registers for specific contexts and practice making polite interjections without interrupting others. The focus is on practical application in fictional spoken scenarios.

objectives.text: Use appropriate phrases and registers, and adapt contributions to take account of purpose, audience and medium.
Respect the turn-taking rights of others during discussions, using the appropriate language for interjections.

sections.heading: Understanding Register and Audience
sections.body: Choosing the right words depends on who you are speaking to and how you are communicating. A formal meeting can call for different language from a casual chat with friends. On the phone, clear wording can be especially useful because a listener cannot see facial expressions or gestures. Adapting your tone helps your message suit its intended audience and purpose.

sections.heading: Respecting Turn-Taking Rights
sections.body: Good discussions rely on everyone having a fair chance to speak. Interrupting can make others feel unheard and disrupt the flow of conversation. Instead of cutting in, use polite phrases to signal that you want to add a point. Waiting for a natural pause shows respect for the current speaker and helps maintain a collaborative and positive atmosphere during group interactions.

sections.heading: Making Polite Interjections
sections.body: When a point needs clarification or you have something relevant to add, wait for a suitable pause where possible. Use polite language to signal your contribution. Phrases like ‘if I may add’ or ‘building on that point’ show that you are listening while contributing. This can help you take part without dominating or dismissing another speaker.

practice.prompt: You are speaking to a new colleague during a formal project review. Which phrase best suits this context?
options: I would like to suggest an alternative.
practice.explanation: The formal context of a project review requires professional and polite language.

practice.prompt: A speaker is explaining a complex idea in a community meeting. How can you interject respectfully?
options: Stop, I have a better idea.
Sorry to interrupt, but I have a question.
Let me tell you what to do.
practice.explanation: Apologising for the interruption and stating your intent is the most respectful approach.

practice.prompt: You are on a telephone call with a client who is speaking. What is the best way to wait for your turn?
options: Talk over them to save time.
Wait for a natural pause in their speech.
Hang up if they take too long.
Make loud noises to get attention.
practice.explanation: Waiting for a natural pause respects the speaker's turn-taking rights.

speakingActivity.title: Private Self-Recorded Discussion Practice
speakingActivity.prompt: Practise a response to this colleague: ‘We need clearer notices about the new office policy.’ Acknowledge the point, add one suggestion, then ask a clarifying question about the next steps. Use language that would suit a workplace meeting.
checklist: Did I use professional language suitable for a workplace meeting?
Did I use a polite phrase to show how I would add my point after a suitable pause?
Did I ask a clear question about the next steps?
